prompt: Find the problems in this case study draft.

task.prompt: Mark the lines in this case study draft that cannot be published as written.

segments.text: Client: a regional home-care provider with 900 caregivers.
Logo and name of the client shown on the cover.
segments.issue: Use the client's name and logo only with written permission.

segments.text: Challenge: shift scheduling was done in spreadsheets, causing missed visits.
Result: revenue grew 300% thanks to our app.
segments.issue: Unverified and attributes everything to the app; use measured results the client has confirmed.

segments.text: We built the scheduling and check-in app in 14 weeks.
Screenshot shows real patient names and addresses.
segments.issue: Confidential personal data; use anonymised or dummy data.

segments.text: Missed visits fell from 6% to 2% in the first three months, according to the client's data.

prompt: Order the sections of a case study.

task.prompt: Order these case study sections from top to bottom.
task.explanation: Context, problem, how, what, results, quote. The reader needs the problem before the solution makes sense, and the quote confirms the results.

task.prompt: A fintech client is happy with your work, but their legal team will not allow their name in public material.

steps.question: What do you propose?
options: An anonymised case study ("a UK payments startup") with details they approve
Publish with their name anyway
Drop the case study entirely
Use their name but not their logo
steps.explanation: Anonymised case studies still prove capability for your ICP.

steps.question: You want to include a result: onboarding time fell from 5 days to 1. What must happen?
options: Nothing; you measured it
The client confirms the figure and approves the final text
Round it to look more impressive
Ask your designer to check it
steps.explanation: Published results need the client's confirmation and approval.

prompt: Work out the results for a case study.

task.prompt: Before your project, a client's customer onboarding took 4.5 days on average; now it takes 1.5 days. Monthly support tickets fell from 1,200 to 780. Round to two decimals.
task.explanation: Onboarding: (4.5 − 1.5) ÷ 4.5 = 66.67%. Tickets: (1,200 − 780) ÷ 1,200 = 35%. Show before and after values alongside percentages so readers can judge them.

prompt: Choose which project to write up.

task.prompt: Your agency's ICP for next year is mid-size logistics companies. You can write one case study this quarter.

steps.question: Which project should you choose?
options: Your most visually impressive project, a fashion brand's website
The largest project by revenue, for a bank
A fleet-tracking app for a mid-size logistics firm with measured results and a willing client
A personal side project from your team
steps.explanation: Case studies work when readers see themselves in them; match your ICP and measured results.

steps.question: The logistics client agrees but has only anecdotal results. What do you do?
options: Estimate results yourself
Publish without results
Use industry averages as their results
Work with them to pull before-and-after data from their systems before writing
steps.explanation: Specific, real numbers are what make a case study credible.

prompt: Write the results section of a case study.

task.prompt: Write the "Results" section of a case study from the confirmed facts below. Keep it factual and specific.
task.context: Confirmed by the client: (1) Missed home-care visits fell from 6% to 2% in the first three months. (2) Schedulers save about 10 hours a week each (4 schedulers). (3) 92% of caregivers used the app daily by month two. Quote approved: "For the first time we know every visit happened." – Operations Director

rubric.label: Uses only confirmed facts
rubric.description: Includes the confirmed numbers accurately, with no invented results.

rubric.label: Specific and measurable
rubric.description: Shows before-and-after values and timeframes, not vague claims.

rubric.label: Easy to scan
rubric.description: Short sentences or bullets that a busy reader can take in quickly.

rubric.label: Uses the approved quote
rubric.description: Includes the quote as approved, attributed by role.

task.sampleAnswer:
Results
- Missed visits fell from 6% to 2% within the first three months.
- Each of the four schedulers saves about 10 hours a week, around 40 hours across the team.
- By month two, 92% of caregivers were using the app every day.
"For the first time we know every visit happened." – Operations Director

prompt: What makes a case study most persuasive to a prospect?

options: Long technical descriptions of the stack
A similar client, a clear problem and specific, confirmed results
Many adjectives about the agency's quality
A list of every feature built
mcq.explanation: Prospects look for themselves in the story and for evidence that the result is real.

prompt: Before publishing a case study that names a client, what must you have?

options: A verbal OK from your contact months ago
Nothing, if the project is finished
The client's written approval of the content and use of their name
Approval from your own design team
mcq.explanation: Naming a client and their results requires their explicit approval of the final version.

prompt: A client's result was strong, but partly due to their own marketing campaign. How should the case study present it?

options: Attribute the whole result to your work
Leave out the result
Inflate it to make up for sharing credit
Report the result honestly and describe your part in it accurately
mcq.explanation: Overclaiming is easy to spot and damages credibility; accurate attribution still persuades.
